files.h:
POST /api/agent/v2/runs/stream — the LIVE path for a chat turn.

The durable run and the live stream are two separate concerns, and conflating
them is what made replies crawl:

  DURABLE  A `harness_runs` row is created and claimed before a single token
           is generated. If the tab closes, the request is killed or the
           slice runs out of budget, `finishRun(status: 'queued')` leaves the
           checkpoint behind and the cron worker carries on. Nothing is lost.

  LIVE     The model's stream is piped straight to the browser over SSE
           (`result.toUIMessageStreamResponse()`). No token touches Postgres
           on its way out of the process.

The event log is still written — but once per finished step, by
`persistStep` inside the runner's `onStepFinish`. So a reply that used to
cost ~337 `assistant.text` rows now costs one row per step, and the typing
speed is the model's, not the database's.

The browser treats this stream as the live view and Realtime as the
reconnect path: if the stream dies, the projection (a fold of the log) still
fills the transcript in

Nightly CEO rollup: one small row per tenant per day.

Runs after the EOD digest (see vercel.json) so it summarises a day that has actually finished.
Idempotent by construction — the primary key is (user_id, day), so a retry or a double invocation
updates the same row instead of appending a second one.

It counts, it does not copy: agent_events and routine_runs can be millions of rows across tenants,
and the whole reason this table exists is to stop the CEO tab depending on their size.

How a launched campaign is configured on Meta, in one place.

WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
The launcher used to decide targeting in three different ways that each drifted
away from what Meta actually accepts:

  1. every ad set carried `location_types: ["home"]` — "People living in this

files.h:
The one place that decides what a launched campaign actually IS.

WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
Before this, three things were decided in three different places and disagreed:
  - the ads modal collected a gender that was sent and then silently dropped;
  - the immediate lead-form fields were hardcoded to Name + Phone + Email, so every
    campaign paid for an email field nobody used and skipped the City that the
    CRM filters on;
  - the objective / optimisation goal was re-derived inline in
    `utils/campaign-processor.ts`, which meant "optimise for conversions" was a
    boolean that only ever reached one branch and no UI could expose the others.

This module is PURE: rows and strings in, a plan out. No database, no network, so
every rule below is testable and the modal and the server can share exactly one
definition of "what the client picked".

Used by:
  - app/dashboard/ads/page.tsx       (renders the goal picker and the field chips)
  - utils/campaign-processor.ts      (turns the plan into real Meta payloads)
  - app/api/meta-ads/launch-campaign (parses what the modal sent)

files.h:
Read an image's dimensions, and say whether it can actually be advertised.

WHY THIS EXISTS
Meta accepts almost any image and then complains later, in `issues_info`, with
something like "The 191x100 crop key for image ads is deprecated" (2490085) or a
low-coverage warning nobody reads. The advertiser's experience is: the campaign
"launched", and then an ad silently fails to serve.

The checks here are deliberately split:
  - `readImageSize` parses the header of a PNG / JPEG / GIF / WebP buffer. No
    dependency, no decoding, no network — 32 bytes of PNG tell us everything.
  - `checkCreative` compares that against Meta's own placement limits and returns
    `blocked` only for an image Meta is certain to refuse, `warning` for one that
    will serve badly in some placements, `ok` otherwise.

Blocking is intentionally conservative. A launch must not be stopped because our
header parser could not read a file; it is stopped only when we are certain.

files.h:
Closing the loop: what ran, how it did, and what the next creative should argue instead.

THE GAP THIS FILLS
The platform could already JUDGE an ad — `recommendOptimisation` reads spend, CTR and frequency and says
pause this, keep that. What it could not do was LEARN. Nothing joined "this creative argued the offer"
to "and it brought leads at half the cost of the one that argued authority", so every new batch started
from zero and the owner paid to rediscover the same lesson every month.

DESIGNED STATELESS ON PURPOSE
There is no learnings table and no learnings cache. Everything here is a PURE function of two things we
already own: the launches we recorded (`campaign_jobs.payload.creativePlan`) and the numbers Meta
returns. Three properties fall out of that, and they are the reason for the choice:

  NO MIGRATION.        Nothing to deploy, nothing to backfill, no schema to keep in sync.
  NO LOST UPDATES.     A cache written by two readers at once silently loses one of them. A value
                       recomputed from source cannot: two runs on the same numbers agree exactly.

Ad copy the platform will actually accept, and copy a human would not be embarrassed by.

WHY THIS IS CODE AND NOT A PARAGRAPH IN A SKILL
The vendored `ad-creative` skill states the character limits and names the phrases that make copy
read as machine-written. Prose is how the agent is TOLD; this is how the product KNOWS. The
difference is not pedantry — it is the one that has already bitten this repo twice:

  - `lib/agent/tools/ads.ts` has carried `describe('Max 40 characters')` on the Meta headline
    since the launcher was written. That is advice to a model, not a limit. A 51-character
    headline passes the schema, gets sent, and Meta truncates it mid-word with no error. The
    advertiser finds out when a customer reads "...starting at ₹85,00,0".
  - Nothing anywhere checked for the copy tics the skill bans. Generate thirty creatives a day
    and the batch multiplies its first draft's habit thirty times: every ad opening on "Unlock",
    every offer "reimagined", every third line an em dash.

WHY THIS EXISTS
The ads code pinned a version at each call site: `v19.0` in the campaign
processor and the ads routes, `v20.0` for interest search, `v21.0` in the agent's
Meta tools — three versions live at once, all of them several releases behind
(Meta is on v27.0 today). A version that still answers is not a version that is
supported: Meta retires roughly two years after release, and when v19 goes the
launcher stops creating campaigns with no code change on our side.

Everything that builds or reads an ad campaign now imports this, so a bump is one
line, and the payloads were exercised against this exact version with
`execution_options: ["validate_only"]` before shipping.

WhatsApp Cloud API calls stay on their own version on purpose: they are a
different product surface with a different deprecation track.

files.h:
One click must not create two campaigns.

WHY THIS EXISTS
The launch button posted a job and returned. Nothing checked whether the same
campaign had just been requested — a double click, a browser retry, or a user who
pressed Launch again because the first response took four seconds all produced a
second campaign, a second ad set, a second set of ads, and a second draw on the
client's launch credits. On a ₹500/day budget that is real money spent twice.

The fingerprint is built only from the things that make two launches "the same
campaign": who it is for, what it is called, the budget, the goal, the creative and
the places it targets. Anything the client changed — a different budget, one more
creative, another city — is deliberately a different campaign.

What "approved" means, and what the API is allowed to say about it.

THE BUG THIS REPLACES
POST /api/agent/v2/action used to answer an approval with invented execution results:

  whatsapp_broadcast -> "Successfully launched WhatsApp broadcast to 400 leads."
  bulk_call          -> "Queued 400 leads for autonomous voice followup."
  anything else      -> "Custom action executed successfully."

None of it was true. No broadcast was dispatched, no call was queued, and nothing at all
happened for an ad spend — the route only flipped a row's status and wrote a sentence. Two
ways to be wrong, both bad: an owner is told a message reached 400 real people when it did
not, and — for the one action type that spends money — the app reports a launch that never
occurred. A user who checks finds the lie and stops trusting every other number.

WHAT APPROVING ACTUALLY DOES
It unlocks the review gate: the event is marked `approved`, the client puts the staged
instruction back into the conversation, and the AGENT performs the work with its real tools.

This business's own normal — so an insight can say "compared to what?".

THE PROBLEM WITH A THRESHOLD
The engine's rules fire on fixed numbers: cost per enquiry above ₹500, connect rate below 40%. Those numbers
were chosen by us, for nobody in particular. For a business whose enquiries cost ₹200, ₹500 is a disaster
that never triggers; for one whose enquiries cost ₹2,000, it fires every single day until the owner stops
reading. A threshold cannot know what normal is for this business, and an analyst who does not know that is
just a traffic light.

WHAT A BASELINE IS HERE
The median of the last N weeks of the SAME metric, computed from the figures we already own. Median, not
mean: one Diwali week with three times the volume should not raise the bar so high that a good week looks
bad, and one dead week should not lower it. Pure and recomputed from source on every read — same reasoning
as `creative-learning.ts`: no table to drift, no cache to lose, two runs on the same data agree exactly.

The CEO's daily findings: what the numbers say, what it means, and what we would do about
it — reported, never done.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
Not an agent that acts. The owner was explicit: the CEO should "only give findings and
reports". So every entry here ends in a *recommendation*, and anything that would spend
money or message a customer is marked `needsReview`, which puts it behind the review gate
rather than in a queue that runs itself. A daily report that quietly launches things is

"Your cost per lead is high" is an opinion. "₹4,820 over the last 7 days bought 6 enquiries —

files.h:
Yesterday's numbers, gathered from the tables that actually have them.

THE RULE THAT SHAPED THIS FILE
A report is only as good as its inputs, and a made-up input is worse than a missing one.
So every figure here comes from a column that exists, verified against the live schema —
and where a figure genuinely cannot be sourced (paid spend attribution lives in Meta, not
in a column we have), the reader returns NULL rather than 0. Zero would tell the owner
"no ads are running"; null tells the engine "we do not know", and the engine says nothing.

WHY THE READS ARE INJECTED
The arithmetic is testable; the queries need a database. `MetricsReader` is the seam, so
the gate can drive real mappings with a fake clock and fake rows, and the Supabase
implementation stays thin enough to read in one go.

WINDOW
A day is the calendar day in the business's timezone, not "the last 24 hours": an owner
comparing Monday with Tuesday does not mean "mid-afternoon to mid-afternoon".

files.h:
Plan everything from the business's real state, then execute.

THE PHILOSOPHY THIS ENCODES
The agent should not be handed a blank page and asked to be creative. It should know: who this business is, what it
sells, what it already has, what has worked, what is running right now, how much it can spend, and what the owner
asked for — and only then decide what to make. Tools are the easy half; knowing what to make is the job.

So there are two steps and they are separate on purpose:

  1. ASSEMBLE  every fact we hold about this business and its current state, in one object (no model, just reads).
  2. PLAN      a model turns that context plus the owner's own words into a decision: the objective, the audience,
               the offer angle, exactly which artefacts to make and why, the order to make them in, the assumptions
               it had to make, and the questions only the owner can answer.

The plan is the spine. Everything after it is execution with the tools the agent already has, which is why this file
never touches a tool: a plan that dictates mechanics would be another templ

Model-designed pages: the two design skills decide the composition, then QA decides whether it ships.

WHY THE TEMPLATE HAD TO GO
`buildLandingPage` is deterministic template code: one column, one hero, a fixed list of blocks. It is honest, fast
and repeatable, and it cannot be tasteful — there is no design decision anywhere in it. That is why the owner's
verdict was "I don't think you used any of the skills", and they were right: skills are instructions for a MODEL,
and no model was involved in the design.

So this asks the model to write the page against `scroll-craft` and `ui-ux-pro-max`, then grades the result with
the same artefact QA that blocks bad output everywhere else, and gives the model exactly one correction pass with
the specific failures named. If it still fails, the caller falls back to the template rather than shipping a bad
page — a plain page that passes beats a beautiful one that does not exist.

files.h:
Cron/operator authentication with support for a zero-downtime secret rotation.

Why this exists rather than a plain `=== process.env.CRON_SECRET` check:
Vercel snapshots environment variables per deployment, and its cron
infrastructure sends `Authorization: Bearer <current CRON_SECRET>`. So if you
change the value, the live deployment still holds the OLD value while the
header carries the NEW one — every cron call 401s until a new deployment
takes over.

Accepting two secrets removes that window:

  1. Set `CRON_SECRET` = old and `CRON_SECRET_NEXT` = new, then deploy.
     Both values are now in the deployment's snapshot; cron still sends old. ✓
  2. Set `CRON_SECRET` = new, delete `CRON_SECRET_NEXT`, deploy again.
     During the gap the live deployment sends new and — because its snapshot
     still holds NEXT = new — accepts it. ✓  No 401 window.
  3. Afterwards the deployment carries only the new secret.

files.h:
Exactly-once side effects for durable runs.

The failure this prevents: a slice executes a tool that sends a WhatsApp
message or launches an ad campaign, then dies before the checkpoint is saved.
On resume the model re-issues that tool call — and without a ledger it would
fire a second time, spending real money and messaging real people twice.

Mechanism (the standard "activity idempotency key" approach):
  key = hash(run_id, tool_name, normalised input)
  - already `completed`/`failed` → replay the stored outcome, never re-execute
  - `started` and fresh             → another slice owns it; retry later
  - `started` and stale             → outcome unknown: refuse to retry, and
                                      dead-letter the run for human review

Only side-effecting tools are wrapped. Read-only tools re-run freely, which
keeps repeated identical reads working normally.

files.h:
Executes one bounded slice of a durable run.

A slice stops when:
  - the model finishes its answer             → run completed
  - the step cap or the time budget is hit    → run re-queued with a checkpoint
  - the owner asked to cancel                 → run cancelled
  - a transient error occurred                → re-queued with exponential backoff
  - retries are exhausted, or a side effect   → dead-lettered for human review
    may have half-executed

Three production guarantees live here:
  * checkpoints make a slice resumable
  * the idempotency ledger makes side effects at-most-once per run
  * backoff + attempts + dead-letter stop a broken run from spinning forever

── the wire and the log are different things ──────────────────────────────
This module used to write every streaming delta into `harness_events` so the
browser could render it over Realtime. That made typing speed a function of
Postgres insert throughput plus Realtime fan-out (measured: ~1 token/second,

Discovery-based tool exposure.

The problem this solves: every tool schema in the registry was sent with every model request.
Measured, that was 67,000 characters across 58 tools — roughly 17,000 tokens of preamble before
the person's first word, on a request as small as "hi". It cost money on every turn, added latency

the model finds it by asking rather than by carrying it.

WHEN a routine actually runs.

THE BUG THIS FIXES
`nextRunAfter()` decided the next slot by adding days to *now*:

    const next = new Date(now); next.setUTCDate(next.getUTCDate() + stepDays);

It never read `run_at_hour` and never read `timezone`. So a routine whose row says
"weekly at 18:00 Asia/Kolkata" fired at whatever clock time it happened to be created or last
bumped, and `run_at_hour` was decoration — a number the UI showed, the CEO tab accepted and the
agent would happily confirm, that the scheduler never looked at. That is worse than not offering
the control: the owner sets 6pm, is told 6pm, and the work appears at 11am.

WHAT THIS DOES
Resolves the next occurrence at the routine's own wall-clock hour in its own timezone, stepping by
its cadence, correctly across DST (the offset is measured at the candidate instant, twice, rather
than assumed once).

Pure: no database, no clock of its own, so the arithmetic is testable against fixed instants.

The problem it solves: on the Hobby plan a sandbox is killed after 1 hour of

files.h:
The raw-response cache: R2, keyed by a hash of the URL **and the definition
version**, with a TTL.

Two things that look like details and are not:

 1. THE DEFINITION VERSION IS IN THE KEY. A page cached by `headlines@v1` is
    not a valid cache entry for `headlines@v2`: the second definition exists
    precisely because the first one extracted the wrong thing. Keying on the
    URL alone would serve yesterday's parse of a changed definition and make
    the diff a lie.

 2. THE BODY IS STORED RAW. Extraction runs on every request against the
    cached bytes, so a definition can be re-run and diffed inside the cache
    window without touching the host again — and a parse bug does not require
    re-scraping a site to fix.

The envelope carries `expiresAt`, so the TTL survives the process: a body
cached an hour ago is not served just because this worker has never seen it.

R2 access reuses the app's single S3 client in `utils/r2.ts` (no second
client, no second credential path), imported lazily so this module — and the
offline verification — never needs AWS in scope.

The polite fetch: SSRF guard → robots → rate-limit wait → one honest request →
classify → retry ONLY on 429/5xx.

This runs server-side, which is exactly why the guard exists: a caller-supplied
URL that resolves to `127.0.0.1`, `169.254.169.254` or a `file:` path turns a
scraper into a way to read the box it runs on. So the URL is validated TWICE —
before the first request and at every redirect hop — and a hostname is resolved
to its addresses and rejected if ANY of them is private, because a name that
points at both a public and a private address is not a public name.

The refusals, and what each means:

  robots     the host said no. No request is made. Not a warning, not a retry.
  ssrf       scheme/host is not something we fetch (file:, data:, private IP).
  login      200 that is really a sign-in page.
  captcha    200 that is really a challenge page.
  auth       401/403 — the host is refusing our unauthenticated request.
  redirect   a hop we refuse to follow (private address, scheme change).

the four seams it is handed. Everything it wires together already refuses the
right things on its own:

files.h:
Per-host politeness: a token bucket, a `Retry-After` memory, and a queue that
guarantees ONE in-flight request per host.

Why all three, and not just a sleep:
 - A token bucket is the only shape that lets a burst of N be honest about a
   sustained rate. Sleeping `1/rps` between calls is the same thing at burst 1,
   and worse for a host that publishes `Crawl-delay: 30`.
 - A `429` is not an invitation to retry immediately. `noteRetryAfter()` parks
   the whole host until the server said it was ready, so one worker's 429
   slows every other worker pointed at that host instead of piling on.
 - Two requests in flight to the same host is the difference between "polite"
   and "a scraper". The per-host chain serialises them, so a definition with
   20 URLs on one host behaves like a reader, not a flood.

`now` and `sleep` are injected. That is what makes "it waited 4.2 s" testable
in a few milliseconds, and it is why the delays in a verification run are the
delays the limiter actually planned, not a second implementation of them.

files.h:
`robots.txt`: fetch it, parse it, cache the parse, and answer `isAllowed`.

A refusal here is a HARD refusal. `RobotsGate.check()` returning
`{ allowed: false }` is the only thing the caller needs to know: the polite
fetcher turns it into a result with no request made at all, never a warning
that proceeds anyway.

WHAT THIS FILE OWNS (and what it deliberately does not)
 - The wire format: `User-agent` / `Allow` / `Disallow` / `Crawl-delay` /
   `Sitemap`, comments, blank-line separated groups, `*` and `$` wildcards.
 - Rule precedence, per RFC 9309 and Google's published behaviour: the
   LONGEST matching pattern wins, and on an equal match `Allow` beats
   `Disallow`. With no matching rule the path is allowed.
 - Which group applies: the token in our own User-Agent that matches a
   `User-agent:` line (e.g. `NobogentScraper`), and `*` when we have none —
   never another vendor's token.
 - A per-host in-memory cache with a TTL, so a hundred-row scrape per host
   reads `robots.txt` once, not a hundred times.

The skill ROUTER: pick the skill that applies, instead of loading all of them.

THE PROBLEM WITH "VENDOR EVERYTHING"
The OpenMontage repository the owner pointed at carries roughly 700 skill files. Loading
them into a turn is not an option: every description costs prompt tokens on EVERY step,
and a catalogue that large makes the model worse at choosing, not better. But not
shipping them at all throws away real knowledge.

THE ANSWER IS A ROUTER, NOT A LIBRARY CARD
  - the prompt carries names and one-line descriptions (progressive disclosure)
  - `pick_skill` scores every available skill against the actual requirement and returns
    the best FEW, with the reason it chose each
  - `get_skill` then loads only the winner's body

So a turn pays for one skill's instructions, not seven hundred.

HOW THE SCORE WORKS, AND WHY IT IS DELIBERATELY SIMPLE
Token overlap between the requirement and the skill's name + description, with a small

can be tested — which matters more here than cleverness, because a ro

The vendored, third-party skills we ship.

Each module in this directory is generated by `scripts/vendor-skills.mjs` from an
upstream MIT-licensed repository, and carries the commit it came from. Nothing here is
hand-edited: `node scripts/vendor-skills.mjs` refreshes, `--check` reports drift.

WHY VENDOR RATHER THAN FETCH AT RUNTIME
A production agent must not depend on GitHub being up, must not pay a network round trip
to read instructions, and must be reproducible â€” the same deploy must answer the same way
next month. Vendoring gives all three, at the cost of a manual refresh, which is a
deliberate price: the content changes only when we choose.

ATTRIBUTION IS PART OF THE CONTRACT
`attribution` on each skill names the repo, the path, the commit and the licence. The
gate (`npm run verify:vendor-skills`) fails if it is missing or if the licence is not on
the allow-list. Removing an attribution to make a test pass is not a fix.

files.h:
Adapt a compiled spec to the footage you actually have.

This is the answer to "I like this style but my clips don't match it". The
honest split is:

  the STYLE is portable  — type treatment, colour, pacing, copy rhythm, the
                           order of information, the shape of the hook and CTA
  the TECHNIQUE is not  — a gimbal walk-and-talk cannot be derived from a
                           locked-off tripod take, and no amount of editing
                           invents camera movement that was never filmed

So adaptation does not try to fake the missing footage. It keeps every portable
decision, swaps each operation for the closest one the assets can actually
support, and records exactly what changed and why — so the result is a deliberate
lighter version of the reference rather than a failed copy of it.

Compile any reference video into an executable spec.

Design changed after reading the HyperFrames `reverse-any-video` skill: our first
version asked a video model for the beat map, and the model invented 15 segments
for a reference that actually has 6 shots — because it was segmenting by text

not exist.

as the original does. The model is then only asked to do what a model is good at:
classify each already-measured shot into our operation vocabulary, and read off
the on-screen text with its timings. Its numbers can no longer move the cut list.

files.h:
Measure a reference instead of trusting a model's description of it.

Borrowed discipline from the HyperFrames `reverse-any-video` skill, which gets
two things right that our compile did not:

 1. Cuts are MEASURED, not inferred. Asking a video model for a beat map gives
    plausible timings; measuring gives real ones. That matters because a spec's
    whole value is its timing, and the skill notes ffmpeg's plain scene score
    misses jump cuts and punch-ins inside a single take.
 2. Verification is NUMERIC. Our only feedback was a Gemini A/B, which scored
    the last build 5.3/10 and got the central occlusion claim flatly wrong.
    A diff that names missing cuts, extra cuts and sound offset cannot be wrong
    in that way.

Both are implemented here against ffmpeg so they run anywhere we already run.

files.h:
Render a spec inside an E2B sandbox instead of on the caller's machine.

Local rendering worked but was bound to one machine's cores. The sandbox gives
a clean Linux box with ffmpeg, more vCPUs than a laptop, and — importantly — the
same environment the app already uses for media work, so this is not a new
dependency, just a new caller.

The properties that make it usable rather than a demo:

 - **Idempotent provisioning.** Toolchain and the 168 MB segmentation model are
   installed once per sandbox and marked with a version file. Warming a cold
   sandbox is the expensive part, so it must never happen twice for the same box.
 - **Content-addressed assets.** Files are downloaded inside the sandbox under a
   hash of their URL and skipped when already present, so re-rendering a revised
   spec does not re-transfer footage.
 - **Validation before transfer.** The output is probed *in* the sandbox for
   duration, frame count and size. A broken render fails there, cheaply, instead
   of after a download.

The spec: what a compiled reference becomes.

A spec is deliberately NOT prose. It references a closed vocabulary of
operations the renderer implements, so a compiled reference can never ask for
something we cannot execute — which is the failure mode that cost two full
re-renders in the earlier attempts (ffmpeg `crop` cannot animate its own w/h;

presenter cannot be built from stills, and the compiler says so instead of

files.h:
The one place vendor spend gets recorded.

Before this module, cost only existed inside an agent turn: the chat route and
the durable runner opened a `UsageMeter` and charged its total at the end. Any
other caller — cron jobs, webhooks, dashboard routes, standalone scripts — hit
Gemini, Kie or E2B and left no record at all. A rough audit found 35 files
calling vendors directly and only 2 of them metered.

So every vendor wrapper calls `recordSpend()`:

  inside a turn  -> accumulate on the turn's meter; the turn charges once at 2x
  outside a turn -> write a `usage_events` row, and charge the attributed user
                    directly (2x), so nothing is both invisible and free

Design rules, learned the hard way:
 - Never throw. Billing must not break a user's task.
 - Record even when we cannot price it (`priced: false`). An unpriced row is a
   countable gap; a missing row is a silent leak.
 - One metering point per vendor call, at the wrapper. Metering again in the
   tool that calls it double-charges the user.

Reading a tool result the way the UI needs to read it.

THE BUG THIS EXISTS FOR
The model reaches most of its tools through a discovery proxy: `call_tool(name,
args)` runs the real tool and returns `{ ok, tool, result }`, so the real
result sits one level DOWN. Every renderer looked for `output.artifact` at the
top level, which meant that for any proxied tool:

  - an approval card was never drawn (WhatsApp send, AI voice call — neither is

    could never appear at all);
  - a question asked through the proxy was never drawn, and the same latent bug
    sat in the question panel;
  - image, audio and video artefacts produced by proxied tools were drawn as a
    bare grey "call tool" row.

The owner then had no way to approve: the gate only unlocks an action whose
approval row says `approved`, and nothing on screen could mark it. The agent
kept staging fresh cards and telling the owner one was on screen.

Both agent tools answered with fiction. `nobogent_whatsapp_send_template` returned

files.h:
The `image` skill's PROMPT BUILDER. Pure: no I/O, no env, no clock, no random.

THE DECISION THIS FILE ENCODES
One call produces one FINISHED image. The prompt below asks for the complete
designed poster — its hero visual AND its typography — in a single render.
The old shape (generate a bare picture, then draw HTML/CSS design elements on
top of it with canvas/sharp/SVG) is banned: it produced a visible composited
seam, type that did not belong to the picture, and text the model never saw.
So nothing here ever asks a model for "a background", for negative space, or
for a place to put type later. `TYPOGRAPHY_CLAUSE` is the line that closes
that door, and `npm run verify:image-skill` asserts it is in every prompt.

WHY THE CLAIM SCAN EXISTS
An image model will happily invent "₹1.2 Cr" because a poster usually has a
price on it. `findUnverifiedClaims` catches a price, a percentage or a phone
number that appears in the brief but not in the supplied facts, and
`buildImagePrompt` refuses rather than shipping an invented number to a
customer. Over-cautious is the correct failure mode here.

compare.ts — reference vs rebuild, as numbers and as frames side by side.

A rebuild is only worth anything if it can be checked against the thing it copied,
so this module answers three questions and refuses to answer them vaguely:

  1. is the runtime the same?   `compareRuntime` — same within ±0.3 s, or the drift.
  2. is the beat count the same? `compareBeats` — every measured onset present, or
     how many went missing.
  3. what do the frames actually look like? `framePairs` picks the timecodes,
     `meanAbsoluteDifference` scores a pair numerically, and
     `contactSheetCommand` writes them side by side (reference LEFT, rebuild
     RIGHT) into one sheet a human can read at a glance.

difference over raw rgb24, plus its share of full scale and a PSNR. It says "these
two frames are 81% different", which is the truth when a rebuild uses the

The intake: what to ask BEFORE writing a beats file.

THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES
A brief is usually one sentence — "make a video like this for my project" with a
reference film attached. From that, a planner has to decide the things that cost
money and cannot be guessed:

  - does the film have people SPEAKING on camera (and so must be lip-synced), or is
    it a narrator over b-roll?
  - who speaks, in what language, while the on-screen copy may be a different one
  - which facts are allowed on screen (a phone number is a promise; so is a price)

files.h:
timing.ts — the measured clock.

The reference film's timing file was never typed by hand: it was derived from
what the voiceover actually did (ffmpeg `silencedetect` on the trimmed wavs,
plus per-chunk pause offsets). This module is that step, made pure and
repeatable:

    onsets (measured)      ->  timing.json (derived)
    [{ id, start, dur }]       { total, vo[], sceneList{}, s1{}, … }

Two rules make the output trustworthy:

 1. The function NEVER invents a duration. It only lays measured lines out on a
    fixed grid (a gap between lines, a lead before the first one) and cuts scene
    boundaries around them. A line that came back 2.66 s long is 2.66 s long.
 2. Every number is rounded once, through `roundTo`, so the same onsets produce
    a byte-identical timing file on any machine — no accumulated float drift
    that would make two "identical" renders differ by a frame.

`s0` is always the 0.5 s plate-only lead-in: a scene on screen at t = 0 never
reveals its non-media `.clip` overlays, so the hook has to be a later scene.

PURE: no I/O, no clock, no randomness.

files.h:
How long and how far a single agent turn may run.

Two separate limits were silently throttling the agent:

 1. `maxDuration = 60` — the platform kills any HTTP request at the declared
    duration. Other heavy routes in this app already declare 300, so 60 was a
    stale default, not a plan ceiling.
 2. `stepCountIs(10)` — the model loop stopped after ten steps no matter how
    much work remained, so any real task was cut off mid-way.

300s is still the practical per-request ceiling on Vercel, so we stop
ourselves slightly earlier: a stream killed by the platform loses the step in
flight, whereas stopping on our own terms means every completed step is
already in the durable session log and can be continued by the next turn.

Usage metering for the agent.

The agent previously charged the user nothing at all — not model tokens, not
sandbox time, not a single Grok video — while an 8s 720p clip alone costs us

files.h:
Where the auth flows are allowed to send someone.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN MODULE
The login page asked Supabase to send password-reset emails pointing at
`/auth/callback?next=/update-password`. No such page has ever existed. The consequence was the worst
shape a bug can take: the email arrived, the link was clicked, the token was VERIFIED and spent, and
only then did the app redirect to a 404 — so the user could not even retry with the same link, and
the app looked broken rather than the route.

    credits = ceil(seconds / 60) × 1   +   seconds × 0.05

files.h:
Reconciliation: did the wallet move by exactly what the work cost?

THE MODEL (already in place, this file only reads it)

  credit_holds         a reservation against one job: `amount`, `spent`, and a
                       state of `open` / `settled` / `released`. A hold never
                       moves money.
  credit_transactions  the ledger. A charge is a NEGATIVE amount; a grant is a
                       positive one. A charge carries `ref = agent_run:<run>:<step>`,
                       uniquely indexed, which is what makes it exactly-once.

So for one run there are two independent records of the same event: the hold's
own `spent` counter, and the sum of the ledger rows that name the run. If those
two disagree, something is wrong and no amount of retrying fixes it — a charge
was applied without updating the hold, or a hold was settled while a ledger row
was rolled back. That is exactly the class of bug that makes a customer's balance
drift away from their receipts, and it is invisible unless something compares the
two. This module does that comparison.

files.h:
First-draft recipes.

These are the "templatisation" the product actually needs: PROMPT-LEVEL
guidance for how to make a sensible, attractive first draft — not a hardcoded
pipeline that dictates which model runs and in what order.

The agent reads the recipe, has its own tools (image model, video model, TTS,
WhatsApp, publishing), and composes the artefact. Recipes are stored in the
playbook, so they can be edited in plain language and versioned like every
other decision.

Design rule: every recipe must define a DEGRADED path. An agent composing from
scratch has more failure modes than a fixed pipeline, so each recipe says what
"still acceptable" looks like when the ideal isn't achievable — otherwise a bad
day produces nothing at all.

files.h:
Playing a call recording without making it public.

THE PROBLEM
The `lead-voice-recordings` bucket was public, and the stream route wrote
`getPublicUrl(...)` into `leads.voice_recording_url`. That means every call
recording of every customer was fetchable by anyone holding the URL, and the URL
is guessable: `<lead id>/vobiz_<provider id>_<timestamp>.mp3`. A public bucket of
customer phone calls is not a storage setting, it is a data leak with a CDN in
front of it.

WHAT REPLACES IT
The bucket is private. A recording is reached with a short-lived signed URL,
created on demand:

  stored value                     -> playable URL
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------
  "<lead>/vobiz_..._123.mp3"        -> signed storage URL (TTL)
  ".../object/public/lead-voice-…"  -> signed storage URL (TTL), path extracted
  "https://media.vobiz.ai/..."      -> null here; the stream route proxies it

Every caller that used to just hand the stored string to a human now goes
through this, so there is one place to reason about the exposure.

files.h:
The daily brief, composed from the playbook instead of from code.

WHAT CHANGED AND WHY
The crons used to BE the pipeline: `auto-generate` decided who ran, when, and
which property; `auto-generate-video` hardcoded the model, the 2x15s chunking,
the stitching and the TTS. That expresses one opinion about how to market a
business, and it is the wrong opinion for a film academy or an immigration
consultancy.

So the day is now described to the agent rather than executed for it. This
module turns

  playbook (positioning, industry, daily_routine, recipes)
+ the routine row (cadence, approval policy, spend ceiling, channels)
+ today's context (date, credits, pending approvals, festivals)

into a brief that says what the day needs and which tools to compose it with.
The recipes are FIRST-DRAFT GUIDANCE, not the implementation: they say what a
good artefact looks like and — critically — what "still acceptable" looks like
when the ideal is not achievable, because an agent composing from scratch has
far more failure modes than a fixed pipeline.

Pure on purpose: no database, no network, no cl

files.h:
The Vobiz calling channels: one place that knows how many calls can be in flight, and which number each one
dials from.

WHY THIS EXISTS
Capacity used to be a number written into the code in two places — `profile.voice_concurrency_limit || 3` in the
dispatcher and another `let maxConcurrent = 3` in the caller — and the DID rotation was separate again. So buying
a fourth Vobiz channel would have changed nothing: the cap would still have been three, and nothing connected
"how many lines we pay for" to "how many calls we place".

A channel here is one concurrent outbound leg with its own caller ID: the auth account it bills to, and the
number it dials from. Capacity is the SUM of the channels' concurrency, so adding a channel is adding an entry
and nothing else — no code change, no second constant to remember.

WHERE CHANNELS COME FROM, in priority order:
  1. `VOBIZ_CHANNELS` — the deployment's own list. Either JSON:
       [{"id":"ch1","authId":"MA_...","number":"+917965480905","concurrent":1}]
     or the compact form, one channel per `;`, `authId:number`:
       "MA_HOSGFZ86:+917965

files.h:
A product's own media: what a business can attach to an offering, and how the agent sees it.

WHY THIS EXISTS
The catalogue said what a business SELLS; the file manager held its FILES. Nothing joined
them, so "make a creative for Batch 12" had no way to reach the photographs of Batch 12,
and the agent either used nothing or used whatever was newest. That is the difference
between a creative that looks like the business and one that looks like a stock photo.

WHAT IS ENFORCED HERE, AND WHY IN CODE
Upload limits live here rather than in a database constraint because they differ by kind
and because a studio owner needs a sentence explaining the refusal, not a 23514 from
Postgres. The numbers are deliberately modest — this is a phone-first product and storage
is the one cost that grows without anybody noticing:

  image     10 MB, 20 per product
  video     50 MB,  5 per product
  document  10 MB, 10 per product

PURE: no upload, no I/O. The caller does the transfer; this decides what is allowed and
describes the result.

files.h:
Multi-value filter normalisation for the CRM "filtered bulk transfer" feature.

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE MODULE
The transfer modal could only pick ONE campaign, ONE pipeline stage and ONE lead form, so
"send every lead from these three campaigns to Priya" meant three passes and three chances to
pick the wrong limit. Widening those three fields to multi-select moves real risk into the query
builder: the API matches a campaign on `campaign_id` OR on `ad_name` (lead-only rows never got a
campaign id), and campaign names in this database genuinely look like

    Hiring | Instant Form | 04-11-2026 / operations executive
    Whatsapp Leads - Nobogent - 02-10-2026 / static - poppy real estate
    "Sarjapur" plots — 2BHK 🏡

Commas, pipes, slashes, quotes and emoji. A PostgREST `or=` tree is comma-separated, so
interpolating that text raw silently turns one honest condition into several different ones
(`ad_name.ilike.%plots — 2BHK 🏡%`, plus a clause per comma) and lets user text restructure the
filter — an injection risk, not just a wrong count. Every value therefore goes through
`pgQuote()`.

The foundation: what each trigger actually hands you, and what each action actually needs.

Every impossible flow we hit came from the same blind spot — a trigger was treated as "an event"
when what matters is the IDENTITY it yields. A Meta ad *click* gives you nothing (no number, no
name); a Meta lead *form* gives you a phone number; an Instagram comment gives you a platform user
id and no phone at all. A WhatsApp message needs a phone number. So comment → WhatsApp is not
"discouraged", it is unrepresentable — and saying so here means every layer above (the flow
builder, the dry run, the MCP read tools) inherits the same truth instead of guessing.

This lives in code because it is domain knowledge about Meta and WhatsApp, not a preference.

files.h:
Flow execution engine: branch-aware traversal and condition evaluation.

The old traversal was a handle-blind BFS from the trigger. It followed EVERY
outgoing edge, so a "Condition" node's true AND false branches both ran, and
"Qualify" could not influence anything. That made the two most-used editor
nodes decorative: a flow could look like it branched while every downstream
step fired regardless.

This module resolves an execution PLAN: an ordered list of nodes to run, with
condition and split nodes deciding which side is reachable at all. The
WhatsApp runner then executes the plan.

Design rules:
 - Deterministic. Same lead + same answers always yields the same branch.
 - Never throw on bad config. A malformed condition is treated as "not met"
   and reported, so one bad node cannot take the whole flow down.
 - Pure. No network, no database — callers pass what they know.

files.h:
Durable waiting, safe sending.

A flow cannot sleep for an hour: the thing executing it has to finish. So a wait is not a pause,
it is a row in a ledger â€” "do step 3 for lead 812 at 09:25" â€” and a clock tick picks up whatever
is due. That is the difference between a flow that can follow up tomorrow and a flow that robocalls
someone at 9:15pm because its 10-second cap clamped the wait.

Every send passes five gates in order, and each one exists because of a real failure mode:
  1. kill switch        â€” the owner can stop every flow at once
  2. opt-out            â€” someone who said stop never gets another message
  3. quiet hours        â€” a due step at 23:40 waits until morning instead of calling
  4. cross-flow freshness â€” another flow messaging this lead minutes ago means this one holds
  5. idempotency        â€” a retried tick cannot send the same step twice

What the watchdog watches.

Every detector here is read-only and returns descriptions. None of them writes anything,
which is deliberate: this is the file you read to know whether the system is looking at

── how a detector earns its place ────────────────────────────────────────────
A condition belongs here when all three are true:
  1. it is invisible to the owner until a customer complains,
  2. it persists (so a 30-minute sweep will still see it),

    is already ignored. Reporting it would have been a permanent false positive. Dropped.

files.h:
One sweep: look, record, fix what is safe, tell the owner what is not.

This is the only place the three halves meet, and the order matters:

  detect  →  record  →  repair  →  resolve  →  notify

Record before repair, always. If the process dies mid-repair there is still an incident row
saying what was attempted, which is the difference between an auditable system and one that
changed a customer's row and left no trace. Resolve after repair so an incident fixed this
sweep is not also marked resolved by the same sweep's bookkeeping. Notify last, because the
message should describe what actually happened, not what was planned.

── one broken detector must not blind the rest ───────────────────────────────
Each detector is called inside its own try/catch. A watchdog whose only failure mode is
"silence because one query started throwing" is worse than no watchdog, because the silence
looks like good news. Failures are collected, returned in the sweep result, and logged.

The incident store: one row per condition, however many times the sweep sees it.

THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES
The sweep runs every 30 minutes. Without identity, a job that has been stuck since
Tuesday is "discovered" 48 times a day, the owner is alerted 48 times, and there is no
way to tell a brand-new fault from the same old one. So every detection gets a
deterministic `fingerprint`, and this module turns "seen again" into an update rather
than an insert.

AUTO-RESOLUTION IS THE OTHER HALF OF SELF-HEALING
A watchdog that only ever adds rows produces a wall of red that nobody reads, and the
owner stops trusting it. So a condition that the detectors no longer report is resolved
automatically, with `resolved_at` as the record. The console then shows what is true now,
not everything that has ever been true.

WHY BATCHED READS AND WRITES
The first live sweep found 36 dead runs sharing one error. A per-row round trip would
have been 36 reads and 36 writes on every sweep, for one condition. Detections are
therefore grouped by cause before they reach here (see `detectors.ts`), and this module

files.h:
The vocabulary of the ops watchdog.

One idea holds this whole system together: **a detector reports, it never acts.**
Detectors only describe what is wrong and what they would do about it. The decision to
act lives in `repairs.ts` behind an allowlist, and the loop that calls both lives in
`healer.ts`. Keeping those three apart is what makes "it fixed something on its own"
auditable instead of mysterious: you can read every detector without reading any repair,
and you can audit every repair without trusting a model.

WHY `blastRadius` SITS ON THE DETECTION AND NOT ON THE REPAIR
The dangerous direction of trust is a detector that quietly widens what may be fixed.
So a detection declares its own blast radius, and the healer refuses to act on anything
that claims `safe` unless a repair is registered for that exact class AND the repair
agrees about the radius. Two independent "yes" answers, from two different files, before
a write reaches production.

Which host is this, and what should it serve?

WHY THIS IS A MODULE AND NOT FIVE LINES IN middleware.ts
It used to be five lines in middleware, and it broke the product in production.

The app domain was recognised by reading `profiles.whitelabel_domain` with the REQUEST'S cookies.
That read is subject to row-level security, which correctly hides other tenants' profiles from a
signed-in user — so for any logged-in visitor the lookup came back empty, the domain was classified
as a customer's custom domain, and every /dashboard page was rewritten into the shared-storefront
routes, which do not exist there. Logged-out visitors were fine (anon can read the whitelabel rows),
which is why the login page kept working and hid the fault: you could sign in, and then everything
404'd.

  1. Hosts that must serve the app shell are configuration, not data. They must never depend on a
     database read that RLS can legitimately hide.

Editing a generated page without re-rolling it.

THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES
`POST /api/landing-page/generate` in `mode: 'edit'` takes `instructions` plus the
whole `currentHtml` and asks a model to return the whole page again. So an owner
who says "change the phone number" gets a NEW page: the hero image is re-picked,

costs a credit, it is not repeatable, and there is no way to prove that the edit

Authentication for calls to our own Cloud Run workers (stitcher, renderer).

Those services are deployed with `--allow-unauthenticated`, because a Cloud Run service
that needs Google ID tokens would force an extra dependency and a credential in the app
just to reach our own container. Instead both containers check a shared secret:

  - container reads WORKER_SECRET and rejects anything that does not match

deployment that has not been given the secret yet. Setting the secret on the containers
is the step that actually closes the door — do that only after the app that sends it is live.

Can the agent actually DO the work we have been building for, from a sentence?

Everything else in this repo proves a PIECE: the reporting gate proves the queries, verify:audiences
proves the matching, verify:broadcast-progress proves the campaign runner. None of that answers the
only question an owner has — "I said a thing in chat; did the right work happen?" — because the agent
is the part that decides which tool to reach for, and it is the part that has failed before (an
earlier run built an audience and then stopped without starting the campaign).

So this drives four ordinary requests through the live chat and checks the WIRING end to end:

  1. a numbers question        → reporting tools, real figures, no invention
  2. "move this lead to X"     → the CRM write lands on the lead, with its history
  3. "fix the footer phone"    → page_read_sections + a page_edit_section APPROVAL CARD,
                                 and the live page is NOT changed while unapproved
  4. "make me an ad image"     → an approval card for generate_ai_image and NO credits spent

files.h:
Can the AGENT do the whole audience -> campaign job, in chat?

The tool-level acceptance (accept:capabilities) proves the functions work. This proves the thing
that matters to an owner: describe the work in a sentence, and it happens — with the one action
that reaches customers stopping for approval instead of firing.

The turn is deliberately ordinary: "make an audience of the leads from THIS campaign, tell me how
many, then send them THIS template". Expected behaviour, in order:
  1. it counts first (preview_audience), because saying "412 people" before tagging 412 leads is
     the difference between a tool and a trap;
  2. it creates the group (create_audience_group), which is free and reversible;

files.h:
Builds the repo snapshot that lets the owner ask "how does X work?" and get an answer from
the real code instead of from a model's imagination.

WHY A SNAPSHOT AND NOT A CHECKOUT
The app runs on Vercel, where there is no `git` and no repository — the deployed bundle is
the only thing present. So the code has to travel with the deployment. This script distils
the tracked source into one JSON file that is committed and bundled, which means the answer
endpoint works at 3am on a machine that has never seen this project.

WHY NOT EMBEDDINGS
`lib/agent/skill-router.ts` already sets the house precedent: deterministic scoring is
instant, free, has no index to go stale, and a search you can explain is a search you can
debug. A codebase this small does not need a vector store — it needs the header comments,
which in this repo are unusually good, matched against the question.

WHAT IS EXTRACTED, AND WHY EACH FIELD EARNS ITS BYTES

  header    the leading block comment, which says what the file is FOR in pros

HARD STOPS (all three, whichever comes first)

  2. --max     (default 100 calls)
  3. 5 consecutive dispatch failures -> abort, something is wrong upstream

files.h:
Apply one SQL migration to the production database, statement by statement.

WHY STATEMENT BY STATEMENT
The management endpoint rejects a whole file that carries many comments, and its
400s come back with an empty body, so a whole-file attempt tells you nothing about
which statement failed. Applying one statement at a time makes the failure land on
a line you can read.

THE CRLF TRAP (this cost a wasted attempt before)
Splitting on ');\n' misses every statement in a CRLF file — the CREATE TABLE
silently never runs and then every dependent index/policy fails 400 for a
legitimate-looking reason. So: strip `--` comment lines, normalise line endings,
then split on ';' followed by end-of-line.

USAGE
  node scripts/db-apply-migration.mjs sql/migrations/19_lead_journey.sql --check
  node scripts/db-apply-migration.mjs sql/migrations/19_lead_journey.sql

--check runs each statement's leading keyword against the catalogue instead of
applying it, so you can see what WOULD happen. Nothing is ever applied without an
explicit run: there is no "did it work?" guesswork and no dry-run that pretends

files.h:
Is the daily job actually making this business better? One table, no adjectives.

WHY THIS EXISTS
"It improves your business daily, based on the numbers" is the promise. Until now there was no
instrument that could confirm or refute it, so the promise was a design intention with a
marketing department attached. This prints, per business, the four things that decide whether
the promise is being kept:

  DAYS RUN      did the job actually run, and did it finish? (the loop is worthless if it dies)
  ENQUIRIES     this week against the week before
  ₹ PER ENQUIRY what the ads cost per enquiry, this week against the week before
  PUBLISHED     what went out, because an engine that makes nothing and reports well is a diary

and then one verdict derived from those, in the same words to every reader: improving, flat,
behind, or not measurable. The verdict uses *both* halves — enquiries up AND cost per enquiry
down or flat — because volume bought with dearer enquiries is not improvement.

It also names jobs that are switched on but have not run in 48 hours, which is the silent
failure mode th

Repair UTF-8 text that was saved after being read as Windows-1252.

The catalogue card rendered "📍 Mexmon Dreams, Jalandhar" as "ðŸ  Mexmon Dreams, Jalandhar", and
several toast messages say "AI Generation Started âœ¨" instead of "✨". Those are not exotic: a file
written with a Latin-1/CP1252 encoder turns each UTF-8 byte into a character, so 📍 (F0 9F 93 8D)
became the four characters "ð Ÿ " and — (E2 80 94) became "â€"".

This reverses it exactly: take a maximal run of characters that could be CP1252 bytes, encode them
back to bytes, decode as UTF-8, and keep the result only when it decodes cleanly (no U+FFFD). A
run that does not decode is left alone, so genuinely non-ASCII text — a Malayalam label, a name
with an accent stored correctly — is never touched.

  node scripts/fix-mojibake.mjs            # report what would change
  node scripts/fix-mojibake.mjs --write    # rewrite the files
  node scripts/fix-mojibake.mjs --all      # include comment lines too

The Nobogent funnel, built for real, as the owner's admin account.

This is the owner's brief taken literally: create everything needed to launch a full marketing funnel for

The video goes through the AGENT's gated tools (a draft render, which the review gate allows on purpose so the

The launch half of the Nobogent funnel: does the agent ASK before spending, and do the flow tools reach a phone?

Three things are tested here, and the first one is the one the owner actually asked about:

  1. ASK, DON'T LAUNCH. A real agent turn is given a deliberately incomplete ad request ("launch a campaign for
     Nobogent, 500 a day"). The correct behaviour is to ask for the facts it cannot know — the audience, the
     creative, the page — and NOT to call a tool that spends money. The turn's own text and tool calls are the
     evidence, printed verbatim.

  2. STAGE, DON'T SPEND. The campaign is created at PAUSED, and the image is uploaded to the ad account so a
     human can finish the build. Nothing is activated. Activation is the one step that needs the owner's word.

  3. A FLOW THAT REACHES A HUMAN. A WhatsApp template and an AI voice call to the only number outbound tests are
     allowed to touch: +918288835235. Anything else is refused by the tools' own test mode.

files.h:
LIVE ACCEPTANCE for the `image` skill — the only place in this package that
spends credits.

  npm run proof:image-skill

It calls the skill exactly as the app does (`createImage`), with nothing
faked except the two things that would touch a customer:

  - `publish` writes the bytes to D:\nobo-images AND puts them on R2 under the
    skill's own key, so the key/URL path is exercised for real;
  - `record` reports `recorded: false` instead of UPDATE-ing `agent_runs` for a
    run row that does not exist.

Everything else is the production path: `createKieImageTask` (kie.ai, real
credits), `queryKieTask`, the real download, and the prompt built by
`lib/agent/tools/skills/image/prompt.ts`.

Ten images, four aspect ratios, four of them editing a supplied reference —
exactly the acceptance the package asks for. C: has ~2.5 GB free on this
machine, so the output lands on D:.

files.h:
Ingest image references into the bank.

Point it at a business whose creatives you want the agent to learn from: it takes that
business's own images, has the vision model describe each one structurally, and banks the
description plus the image URL. The agent then picks one and rebuilds it for whichever
business it is working on — the description is what makes picking cheap.

  npm run ingest:image-ref -- --tenant <uuid> --count 6 --industry "real estate"

Descriptions are structural on purpose: layout, where the copy sits, framing, light, mood.
No brand names, no claims — a reference must never carry a third party's identity forward.

files.h:
Ingest one video into the reference bank.

Measures the file (probe + cut detection + loudness), builds a small proxy and a contact
sheet, uploads both to R2 so the agent can actually look at them, and writes a bank entry
with the measurements attached. One command per reference:

  npx esbuild scripts/ingest-reference-video.ts --bundle --platform=node \
    --format=esm --packages=external --outfile=.tmp-ingest.mjs

  node .tmp-ingest.mjs --file "<path>" --slug homcom-mohali --industry "real estate" \
    --summary "16 bold text beats over stills, dissolves, end card with phone"

files.h:
How fast does a reply actually reach the browser?

Two transports are measurable, and this script measures both against the same
deployment:

  db   — the PREVIOUS design. A turn is queued, and the runner writes the
         growing answer into `harness_events` about four times a second; the
         browser paints whatever Realtime has delivered. Time-to-first-token
         and paint rate are therefore bounded by Postgres + Realtime.

  sse  — the CURRENT design. The model's stream is piped straight to the
         caller and nothing is written per token. Time-to-first-token is the
         model's, and paint rate is the model's token rate.

Run it against the deployment you want to measure, before and after a change:

  npm run measure:stream -- --mode=db           # baseline (old transport)
  npm run measure:stream -- --mode=sse          # new transport
  npm run measure:stream -- --mode=flow          # find_tools -> call_tool -> create_flow

It authenticates as an existing user through a magic link minted with the
service role, so no password is needed and nothing is created for

Does a flow actually reach a person now?

This probe runs the real chain against the real database, in the order production runs it:

  event  → ingress.fireFlowTrigger  (only a real webhook calls this in production)

the honest outcome is `blocked` with the 24-hour reason — which proves the dispatcher ran, applied

files.h:
Rebuild the Procolor ad properly and fix the underlying defect.

The first render came out static: every frame identical. Cause — HyperFrames drives GSAP by seeking
a PAUSED timeline that the page must register on `window.__timelines`; mine created a timeline and
never registered it, so there was nothing to seek. The CLI says so explicitly when duration cannot
be inferred ("No GSAP timeline registered (window.__timelines is empty)").

Design fixes: one line at a time on a clean dark plate, the academy's own cinematic photograph used

LIVE acceptance for the scraping capability. Real network, real servers, a
handful of requests in total.

What it proves, in this order:

 1. RETRY/BACKOFF against a real server that returns 429 (`httpbin.org`), with
    the real clock — the delays printed are the delays it actually waited.
 2. THREE permitted sources scraped for real, each with the robots.txt decision
    quoted verbatim: a public news RSS feed, a standards-body page, and
    `example.com` (whose robots.txt is a 404, i.e. nothing published to obey).
 3. A REFUSAL that is a valid result: `httpbin.org/deny`, which its own
    robots.txt disallows. The page must never be requested.
 4. THE R2 CACHE: the same URL twice, one request, one PUT, one hit — using the
    real bucket when this process has credentials for it.

Request budget: ~6 page requests and ~5 robots.txt reads, one at a time per
host, with `Crawl-delay` honoured where a host publishes one. Nothing here is
login-walled, and nothing is retried past three attempts.

Bluesquare test calls - using the APP'S OWN DEFAULT SCRIPT.

WHY THERE IS NO custom_prompt HERE
The default caller you liked is the bridge's built-in system instruction
(voice-bridge/server.js buildGeminiSetupConfig). It already:
  - reads the lead's form answers, CRM notes, product + catalogue context
  - asks a single discovery question and stops talking
  - defaults to Hinglish and switches language with the caller
  - books a slot via the book_appointment_slot tool

A non-empty custom_prompt is appended as "CAMPAIGN SPECIFIC GUIDELINES" and
overrides all of that - which is exactly what a hand-written script did wrong.
So custom_prompt is deliberately NULL: the route's contextual script and the
bridge's default caller are left untouched.

  audience_filter.voice_name = 'Aoede'          -> female voice

  audience_filter.greeting   = 'Hi {name} ji, kaise ho aap?'

files.h:
Module resolution hooks so plain `node` can load the app's TypeScript sources.

Node 24 strips types natively, but its ESM resolver is strict about
specifiers: `./runner` and `@/utils/r2` do not resolve, so a self-test that
wants to exercise a real module would be limited to files that happen to have
no imports at all. These hooks add the two things the repo's source already
relies on (extensionless relative imports and the `@/*` tsconfig path alias)
without touching a single source file and without adding a dependency.

Usage, before the first import of a .ts file:

  import { register } from 'node:module';
  register('./ts-resolve-hooks.mjs', import.meta.url);

Only resolution is hooked; loading still goes through Node's own TypeScript
type-stripping, so no build step is involved.

Blue Square script updater — v2 with a HARD BOOKING GATE.

WHAT CHANGED FROM v1 AND WHY
v1 said "the goal is a booked slot" and the caller obliged: it booked a site
visit for Hardil/Jojo, whose entire interest was asking about a job
("meri job hai"). That is the exact failure mode of optimising for bookings:
the cheapest way to get a booking is to lower the bar.

v2 makes qualification the gate and the booking the reward:
  - book ONLY when budget AND timeline are captured (now or from prior data)
  - if either is missing, do NOT book; offer a consultant callback instead
  - anything that is not a property purchase (job, vendor, wrong number)
    closes politely and books NOTHING

ASR: five calls today had an Indian prospect transcribed as Portuguese
("obrigado", "Tudo bem"). Gemini Live auto-detects language; the fix that
needs no deploy is to instruct the model explicitly.

Vendor the open-source skills the owner approved, straight from upstream.

WHY A SCRIPT AND NOT PASTED FILES
These are ~60 KB of somebody else's writing. Copying them by hand invites silent
drift: a typo in one word, a section quietly dropped, no way to tell which upstream
commit you are running. This script downloads each file, records the commit and the
licence beside it, and writes a typed module. Re-running it REFRESHES the vendored
copies, and the gate fails if any of them has lost its attribution.

LICENCES, VERIFIED NOT ASSUMED
  nateherkai/scroll-craft              MIT
  nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill MIT
  cdeistopened/content-os              MIT
All three permit commercial use with attribution, which is what `attribution` below is
for. If a licence ever stops being MIT, the gate has to be told — not quietly ignored.

  node scripts/vendor-skills.mjs            # refresh every vendored skill
  node scripts/vendor-skills.mjs --check    # report drift against upstream, write nothing

"For GNR Homes" has to work.

WHAT HAPPENED
The owner (super admin) asked for GNR Homes' leads from its latest campaign. The agent could not find
the account. GNR HOMES is an independent client — role admin, no parent, no agency — so it is not in
the caller's subtree, and `query_account_data` only offered me / org / all. There was no way to look an
account up by NAME, and no way to point a read AT one. For a super admin that is simply a broken
answer to a fair question.

  3. live: the directory finds GNR HOMES as super admin and reports its real lead count and latest
     campaign; a different tenant cannot see it; and query_account_data with that accountId returns

Does the AGENT actually have the capability, for a real tenant?

Every earlier gate proved a *library*. This one builds the REAL agent context —
`createAgentContext()`, the same function a live turn calls — for a real tenant in
the real database, and asks, for each thing a customer asks Nobogent to do:

  1. does the conversation select the tool GROUP that capability lives in?
  2. is the specific tool PRESENT in the registry the model would be given?

the group that should have carried it, because "the customer asked for an ad
campaign and the agent had no campaign tool" is the failure that matters, and no

Is the agent at parity with the product - and does it keep the primitives while gaining composed tools?

THE TWO FAILURES THIS COVERS
 1. The agent could not launch ads or call a segment of leads at all. `launch-campaign` / `launch-remarketing` were
    UI-only routes (21 KB and 68 KB of decisions that took real bugs to get right), and the calling campaign runner
    lived only in the dashboard. So "run me a retargeting campaign" and "call my 400 Diwali leads" were answered
    with improvisation or a pointer to the dashboard.
 2. The obvious fix - bolt on composed tools - has its own failure mode: a composed tool that becomes the ONLY way,
    so anything Meta allows and the wrapper does not expose becomes impossible. The primitives must stay.

processor; AND the primitives are still registered, still mentioned, and the prompt forbids refusing on the grounds
that no composed tool fits.

files.h:
Does the agent UI survive being switched to dark mode?

WHY THIS EXISTS
Dark mode was broken in a way no amount of staring at one screen would have proven:
`lib/ui/agent-skin.css` defined its entire palette under `.dsh[data-theme='light']` and
wrote the component rules under that same selector too. So in dark mode the skin was not
"slightly wrong" — it was not applied at all. `--nobo-card` was undefined, the two rules
that used a literal `#ffffff` stayed white, and every structural rule (tap feedback, focus
ring, 44px targets, the sticky composer) silently stopped existing. On top of that,
`CeoFindingsCard` was built from Tailwind `dark:` pairs, which key off the OS colour scheme
and not off `data-theme`, so they always resolved to their light branch.

That is a class of bug, not an incident: the theme is a second axis nobody was testing, so
every new rule could silently pick the wrong one and nothing would say so. These checks
make the class impossible to reintroduce quietly:

  1. BOTH PALETTES EXIST, and declare the same token names. A token defined in only one
     theme is undef

Can a gated tool be resumed with ONLY an approvalId?

The review gate tells the model, and buildResumePrompt tells it again in stronger words: "call the
tool again and pass this approvalId. The approved arguments are used verbatim, so do NOT re-type or
re-word the payload." That is only true if the schema ACCEPTS a call carrying nothing but the id.

A live video run suggests it is not: `generate_voiceover { approvalId }` produced no tool result at
all, the agent gave up on the voice, and the delivered film came out silent. If the tool's own
required fields are still required, the call never reaches `execute` — so the approved args are
never replayed and the instruction is a trap.

files.h:
Proves the approval card can actually continue the job.

THE FAILURE THIS PINS
Tapping Approve in production recorded the decision and then nothing happened. The card said
"Approved & in progress", the row flipped to `approved`, and no run was ever created — the
work never started. The cause was a single dropped prop: the durable transcript (the DEFAULT
render path) accepted `onOptionSelect` but not `onResume`, so the card had no way to hand the
staged instruction back to the conversation.

Every approval on the default path was a dead end, and nothing caught it because each unit
worked in isolation: the card resumed correctly when a handler was passed, and the handler was
correct when it was called. The wire between them was missing.

So this gate checks the WIRE, at every render site, not the units.

files.h:
ONE APPROVAL ROUND TRIP, ONE REAL WHATSAPP.

The complaint this closes: "approve used to do nothing". The unit gates prove the pieces
separately — verify:review-gate proves the gate refuses and records, verify:approval-loop-live
proves an approved id runs its exact call — and verify:outbound-live proves the channel reaches
the owner. None of them proves the whole sentence: that a message the owner approved is the
message that a real customer-facing provider then accepted, with nothing recited from a summary.

So this runs all five steps against the real database and the real Graph API:

  1. call the GATED tool with no approval   -> it must REFUSE and record a card
  2. read the recorded row                  -> it must hold the tool's exact arguments
  3. approve it the way the UI's tap does   -> mark the event approved
  4. call the tool again with only approvalId -> the approved arguments must be replayed
  5. re-read the row                        -> it must be SPENT (status 'used'), not still valid

Step 5 is the one that stops an approval authorising the same send over and over.

Do the auth links actually land somewhere that exists?

THE BUG THIS WOULD HAVE CAUGHT
The login page asked Supabase to put `next=/update-password` in every password-reset email. There is
no such page in this app — the reset form is `/auth/reset-password`. So the flow was: email arrives,
link clicked, token VERIFIED and spent, and only then a redirect to a 404. The user could not retry
with the same link, and the app looked broken rather than the route.

Two kinds of assertion here, because the source-level one alone would not have caught it:
  - the destination rules (safeNext / isRecoveryTarget) behave, including for the dead path that old
    emails still carry;
  - EVERY literal auth destination in the app resolves to a page.tsx or route.ts ON DISK. That is the
    check that turns "the route was never built" from a production 404 into a failing gate.

  npm run verify:auth-links

Read-only: reads source, writes nothing, touches no network.

files.h:
Does the agent actually keep working with nobody watching?

The point of durable runs is that closing the app, reloading, or losing the tab does
not stop the work: a background worker claims the run from a queue and advances it
server-side. "Reattach on return" is only the visible half — the half that matters is
that progress happens with no client connected at all.

These checks drive the queue primitives directly, so they prove the background
machinery without spending on model turns:

  1. a queued run is picked up by a worker with no browser involved
  2. two workers never take the same run (the SKIP LOCKED claim)
  3. a worker that dies mid-run has its run reclaimed, not lost
  4. retries back off and then dead-letter instead of looping forever

  npm run verify:background

files.h:
Can the owner change how their agent behaves, by saying so?

THE BUG THIS COVERS
The agent could already patch its playbook, but three other pieces of "how this business behaves"
had no path at all:
  1. the routine row (cadence, hour, ceiling, approval policy, on/off) - the agent could start a
     routine and change nothing about it;
  2. the default calling voice / language / auto-call - `createVoiceTools` was written and then
     NEVER imported by the orchestrator, so the tool did not exist for the model at all;
  3. the calling script - the dead tool pointed it at `profiles.custom_prompt`, which is the
     brand's VISUAL STYLE prompt for creatives, so wiring it as written would have silently
     rewritten the art direction of every future image.

So this asserts the wiring (not just that the functions exist), what each write targets, which
phrasing reaches the tools, and which of the writes must come back for approval.

Reads source with comments stripped, because a comment describing a fix must never satisfy the
test for that fix.

files.h:
The filtered bulk transfer's multi-select filters: does the query we build actually say what the
admin picked?

THE FAILURE THIS IS REALLY ABOUT
"Send every lead from these three campaigns to Priya" used to be impossible — the Campaign filter
held one string. Widening it to an array puts user text (campaign/form names, which in this
database really do contain commas, pipes, slashes, quotes and emoji) inside a PostgREST `or=`
tree, where a comma is a clause separator:

    ad_name.ilike.%Hiring | Instant Form | 04-11-2026 / operations executive%

is fine, but

    ad_name.ilike.%Whatsapp Leads - Nobogent - 02-10-2026 / static - poppy real estate%

is not the danger — the danger is any name with a comma, which silently becomes TWO conditions,
changing what gets transferred while the preview still shows a confident number. So this gate
asserts on the exact expression string handed to PostgREST, clause by clause, and refuses to
accept "it compiles".

Pure: no database, no network. Every case is a value in, a string out.

  npx tsx scripts/verify-bulk-filters.ts

The prompt decided the lead's origin with `source.includes('whatsapp') || custom_fields.meta_ad_origin`.

files.h:
Proves the daily report is written for a business owner, not for a marketer.

WHY THIS GATE EXISTS
The report's first version was technically correct and practically unreadable. It said
"cost per lead has risen" and "40% of calls connected" and "0 routine(s) ran". An owner running
a film academy or a clinic has no reason to know what CPL, CTR or an ad set is, and a report
they cannot read is a report they stop opening — at which point the whole engine is a receipt
nobody collects.

So the plain-language rule is not a style preference, it is a product requirement with the same
standing as "never invent a number". These checks fail the build on:

  1. JARGON in any owner-facing string: acronyms, terms of art, and percentages.
  2. A NUMBER WITH NOTHING TO COMPARE IT TO — "12 enquiries" is trivia; "12 enquiries, 4 more
     than the week before" is information. Where a previous value exists, the sentence must use it.
  3. AN EMPTY OR VAGUE RECOMMENDATION. Every finding has to end in something a person can say
     yes to.
  4. INTERNAL NAMES leaking into the interface ("Daily engine", "

files.h:
The creative doctrine the owner asked for, asserted against the prompt the model actually receives.

Four rules, each of which changes what the agent DOES rather than what it says:

  1. REFERENCES ARE THE DEFAULT. The owner should not have to ask for one — especially for images. If
     they pass one, that one wins; otherwise the agent goes and finds one before writing a prompt.
  2. VIDEO IS SCRIPT-FIRST. Script -> shot list -> per-shot decision about AI footage vs free stock ->
     build. Not "generate a clip and hope".
  3. A SUPPLIED VIDEO IS WATCHED FIRST, before any decision is taken.
  4. NO SPEAKING PERSON by default — TTS narration (Gemini 3.8 Flash). A generated presenter only when
     explicitly asked for, and then via Grok inside the film.

§0 of the brief: "when I ask for a video it makes a video with voice and music". Voice works.

files.h:
Proves a business cannot be charged twice for the same day's routine, and that a run with no
instruction is refused at the door instead of dead-lettered in the worker.

WHY THIS GATE EXISTS
Two separate bugs combined to make duplicate work invisible:

  1. Nothing stopped a business holding several `business_routines` rows, and the routine-run
     idempotency key is `(routine_id, period_key)` — per routine, not per business. So every
     extra row bought another run for the same day with its own key. Measured: six runs for one
     tenant on 2026-11-12.
  2. A run could be queued with no instruction at all, which the worker dead-lettered silently
     30 seconds later in another process — `attempts: 0`, nothing thrown, nobody told.

The fixes are a pure picker, a pure validator, three call-site guards and two database
constraints. This gate pins the pure halves and the guards; the constraints are proven by
`scratch/prove-routine-constraints.mjs` against the live database.

  npm run verify:routine-once-per-day
